summary: This document defines Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) extensions for grouping two unidirectional MPLS-TE Label Switched Paths, one in each direction, into an associated bidirectional LSP. It works with a stateful PCE for both PCE-initiated and PCC-initiated LSPs, or a stateless PCE, and applies to LSPs signaled with RSVP-TE.

eli5.summary: One-way streets can be paired into a two-way road. This document gives a path planning protocol a way to say that two one-way paths in opposite directions belong together as a pair.

subtitle: How a path computation server can tell routers that two one-way MPLS-TE paths belong together as one two-way path.

tldr.problem: MPLS-TE paths (LSPs) run in one direction only, but some networks need a two-way path made of a forward and a reverse LSP. RSVP-TE can bind the two, but PCEP had no way to describe that pairing to a Path Computation Element (PCE).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two Association Types (single-sided and double-sided) to the PCEP ASSOCIATION object, plus an optional Bidirectional LSP Association Group TLV with a Reverse (R) flag and a Co-routed (C) flag.
tldr.outcome: A stateful or stateless PCE can now create, update and report associated bidirectional LSPs for RSVP-TE signaled paths. It is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 9756 updates it.

facts.label: Flags
facts.value: R is bit 31, C is bit 30

today: RFC 9059 is a Proposed Standard from June 2021 and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9756. Read the two together when implementing it.

sections.title: Why Pair Two LSPs
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE) cooperate on computing MPLS-TE Label Switched Paths (LSPs). RFC 8231 adds stateful control, and RFC 8281 lets a PCE initiate LSPs. RFC 8697 adds a generic way to group LSPs into associations.

The MPLS Transport Profile requirements say transport paths must support unidirectional, co-routed bidirectional and associated bidirectional forms. RFC 7551 already defines the RSVP signaling for binding a forward and a reverse LSP into an associated bidirectional LSP. This document supplies the missing PCEP side.

The procedures apply to LSPs signaled with RSVP-TE. Pairing Segment Routing paths is explicitly out of scope and is left to a separate draft.
sections.eli5: Imagine two one-way streets that run side by side. A helper who plans routes needs a way to say that these two streets are really one road with a lane each way.

sections.title: Single-Sided and Double-Sided Initiation
sections.content:
An associated bidirectional LSP has a forward LSP and a reverse LSP between the same two endpoint nodes. Following RFC 7551, there are two ways to start one.

In single-sided initiation the bidirectional tunnel is provisioned on only one endpoint, the originating node. Both the forward and reverse LSPs are initiated there. The originating node signals the reverse LSP properties in the RSVP REVERSE_LSP object of the forward LSP Path message, and the remote endpoint then creates the reverse tunnel and signals the reverse LSP.

In double-sided initiation the tunnel is provisioned on both endpoints, and each endpoint initiates its own forward LSP. For fast reroute bypass tunnel assignment, the LSP with the higher source address is treated as the forward LSP.

Either kind can be co-routed, meaning the forward and reverse LSPs follow the same congruent path in their respective directions.

The RFC lists trade-offs. Double-sided lets two existing LSPs in opposite directions be associated without much extra operational complexity. Single-sided suits OAM cases where an endpoint must know both paths, lets the originating PCC compute co-routed paths dynamically, and works where PCEP runs only on the originating endpoints.
sections.eli5: Single-sided is like one person drawing both lanes of the road and telling the other end. Double-sided is like both ends each drawing their own lane and agreeing they belong together.

sections.title: The ASSOCIATION Object and Group TLV
sections.content:
The RFC defines two new Association Types for the generic ASSOCIATION object (Object-Class value 40): Single-Sided Bidirectional LSP Association (4) and Double-Sided Bidirectional LSP Association (5). An LSP, forward or reverse, MUST NOT be in more than one Bidirectional LSP Association, and the two LSPs MUST have matching endpoints in reverse directions. In the single-sided case, both LSPs must be in the same tunnel on the originating node.

Before using these types, a PCEP speaker MUST list them in the ASSOC-Type-List TLV in its OPEN object and MUST receive the same from its peer.

The optional Bidirectional LSP Association Group TLV has Type 54 and a Length of 4 bytes. Its value is a 32-bit Flags field with two defined bits: R (bit 31) marks a reverse LSP and C (bit 30) marks a co-routed bidirectional LSP. If the TLV is missing, the LSP is a forward LSP that is not co-routed. Reverse LSPs MUST carry the TLV with R set, and co-routed LSPs MUST carry it with C set. The TLV MUST NOT appear more than once; only the first occurrence is processed. Unassigned bits MUST be sent as 0 and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: It is like putting a sticker on each path that says which pair it belongs to, plus two little checkboxes: 'this is the way back' and 'this follows the same route as its partner'.

sections.title: PCEP Procedures
sections.content:
The procedures cover three starting points: neither LSP exists yet, both exist but are not yet associated, or one exists and its reverse must be created.

For PCE-initiated LSPs, the PCE sends a PCInitiate message to the originating endpoint with both LSPs (single-sided) or to both endpoints with their forward LSPs (double-sided). PCCs report with PCRpt, and the PCE updates with PCUpd. A stateful PCE adds and removes the association on a per-LSP basis.

For PCC-initiated LSPs, the PCC reports with PCRpt and may delegate LSPs to a stateful PCE. In the single-sided case, the originating PCC SHOULD delegate the forward and reverse LSPs together to avoid a race condition.

A stateless PCE can be asked to compute co-routed or non-co-routed forward and reverse paths for a request tied to an association group. The Bidirectional (B) flag in the RP object is also set when the PCC wants the same TE requirements in both directions.

Other rules: in the single-sided case the reverse LSP gets two different PLSP-IDs, one at the ingress PCC and one at the egress PCC. The LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV MUST be included in all forward and reverse LSPs. During state synchronization, a PCC MUST report all existing Bidirectional LSP Associations, and the PCE MUST then remove any previous ones absent from the report.
sections.eli5: Either the planner or the router can start the pairing. Whoever starts it tells the other side about both halves, and everyone keeps a list so nothing gets lost when they re-check.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
A PCE speaker that sees a broken pairing MUST answer with a PCErr message of Error-Type 26 (Association Error). Each kind of mistake gets its own Error-value, as shown below.

The RFC also says the PCEP Path Setup Type for these associations must be RSVP-TE (value 0), and any other value triggers the Path Setup Type error. The rules in Section 6.4 of RFC 8697 continue to apply.
sections.eli5: If someone tries to pair two paths in a way that does not make sense, the receiver sends back a note saying exactly what is wrong.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 apply. The new Association Types also inherit the risks from a malicious PCEP speaker described in RFC 8697, so securing the PCEP session with TLS (RFC 8253) is RECOMMENDED.

On manageability, the RFC says it adds no new control, liveness, verification or network-impact requirements beyond those of the earlier PCEP documents. There are no new MIB objects, and a PCEP YANG module is cited as the data model for LSP associations.
sections.eli5: Because a bad helper could try to mix up the pairs, the RFC says to lock the conversation with encryption.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned values 4 and 5 in the ASSOCIATION Type Field subregistry, and value 54 in the PCEP TLV Type Indicators subregistry for the Bidirectional LSP Association Group TLV.

IANA also created a new subregistry for the TLV's Flags field, with bits 0 to 29 unassigned, bit 30 for C and bit 31 for R. New values there are assigned by Standards Action. Six new Error-values, 14 to 19, were added under Error-Type 26 (Association Error).
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got new entries so every router uses the same number for the same thing.

items.label: Association group mismatch
items.desc: An LSP is in more than one Bidirectional LSP Association.

items.label: Tunnel mismatch in the association group
items.desc: A single-sided association gets an LSP from a different tunnel.

items.label: Path Setup Type not supported
items.desc: The Path Setup Type is not RSVP-TE.

items.label: Bidirectional LSP direction mismatch
items.desc: Both LSPs are forward or both are reverse.

items.label: Bidirectional LSP co-routed mismatch
items.desc: One LSP is co-routed and the other is not.

items.label: Endpoint mismatch in the association group
items.desc: The endpoints do not match in reverse directions.
